title: What's the Difference Between an A-Player and the B's & C's
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article offers a simple, working definition to distinguish A, B, and C players by how much scaffolding they need: A-players need only a goal, B-players need a goal plus a strategy, and C-players need the goal, strategy, and specific tactics spelled out. It acknowledges the framework is a simplification but argues it usefully matches most leaders' lived experience of their teams. Rather than treating the grades as fixed, the piece turns the framework into a development roadmap, recommending specific practices — dissecting strategies for B-players, prioritizing tactics for C-players — to help each group climb toward the next level. It closes with the memorable claim that developing lower-graded talent is as much a mark of good leadership as recruiting A-players in the first place.
points: A-players need only a goal; B-players need the goal plus a strategy; C-players need goal, strategy, and specific tactics — a simple diagnostic for coaching gaps.
B-players develop by practicing the construction and dissection of strategies and approaches to problems, not just executing given ones.
C-players develop by identifying and prioritizing the tactical steps within a given strategy, building the connective tissue they currently lack.
Good leaders are framed as those who develop C- and B-players upward, not just those who recruit A-players.
quotes: Here's a simple scheme: A-players just need a goal. Once they know the desired outcome, they can figure out how to get there.
B-players need the goal and the strategy or approach to achieve it. They depend on leaders to help them think through the various choices or options and what game plan is best to ensure success.
C-players need more than the goal and the strategy. They need the tactics, too.

B-players need practice thinking of strategies and approaches to problems and goals. Dissecting existing strategies and creating new ones is how B-players gain the confidence and acumen to fly on their own.
Good leaders do more than simply recruit A-players to join their teams. They do the hard work it takes to elevate the talents, skills, and potential of everyone on the team, including the C-players.
